catalog_quote: Brainard 1991 p.190: 'There are nineteen phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: fourteen consonants and five vowels. ... Word stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.' SIL fact sheet: 'Stress is phonemic, but is marked only in the dictionary.' Olson et al. 2008 p.143: 'two adjacent identical consonants represent a long consonant. We write them as two consonants in order to allow for stress to be marked properly on forms such as item 33: abobba [abobˈba] ‘short’. Second, two adjacent identical vowels represent two distinct vowels occurring in separate syllables, such as in item 20: poos [ˈpoos] ‘few’.' Wordlist p.144: '2. you sing.; thou sika [ˈsiʔa] 3. he siya [siˈja] ... 6. they dida [diˈda]'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated locator in the held files (Brainard 1991 p.190; SIL fact sheet first spelling rule; Olson et al. 2008 pp.143-144). sources.citation: Brainard, Sherri (comp.). 1985. Upper Tanudan Kalinga texts. Studies in Philippine Linguistics Supplementary Series: Philippine Texts 1. Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines and SIL. ix+126 pp. (SIL archive entry 25798; fetched sources front matter, pp.1-13, 117-126 via Wayback)
sources.quote: 'There are 19 phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: 14 consonants and 5 vowels. The consonants are /p,t,k,b,d,g,m,n,ng,s,l,w,y/ and glottal stop. The vowels are /i,u,o,e,a/. Stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.' No positional or weight rule anywhere in the fetched sources pages; the Introduction (p.vii) has no phonology content.
